one.text: A Bloom filter answers one question: is this item in the set? It never stores the items, only a row of bits, so it stays tiny: about ten bits per item for a one percent error rate, however long the items are. That makes it a cheap first check: a database can skip a disk read whenever the filter says no. The price is that it can say maybe when the truth is no. Here are sixteen bits, all zero, and one hash function.
To add cat, each hash function turns the word into a big number, and the remainder after dividing by sixteen picks a bit. Its bit, bit six, becomes one.
Now fox. Its bit, bit three, becomes one.
Now owl. Its bit, bit four, becomes one. The filter now holds three ones, and no words at all.
Now a question. Is fox in the set? Hash it the same way. bit three is one, so the answer is maybe. And it's right: fox was added.
Is elk in the set? bit zero is zero. If elk had been added, that bit would be one. So the answer is definitely not. As long as no bit is ever cleared, that answer is always right.

Jay was never added. But its bit, bit six, was set by another word. So the filter says maybe. That's a false positive: the one kind of mistake a Bloom filter makes. The more bits are set, the more often it happens.
There's no delete in a Bloom filter. Suppose we clear cat's bits anyway. This time no other word used them, but the filter has no way to know that.
Now a question. Is fox in the set? Hash it the same way. bit three is one, so the answer is maybe. And it's right: fox was added.

three.text: A Bloom filter answers one question: is this item in the set? It never stores the items, only a row of bits, so it stays tiny: about ten bits per item for a one percent error rate, however long the items are. That makes it a cheap first check: a database can skip a disk read whenever the filter says no. The price is that it can say maybe when the truth is no. Here are sixteen bits, all zero, and three hash functions.
To add cat, each hash function turns the word into a big number, and the remainder after dividing by sixteen picks a bit. Its bits, bit six, bit twelve and bit fifteen, become one.
Now fox. Its bits, bit three, bit five and bit six, become one. bit six was already one, set by cat. So fox now shares bits with cat.
Now owl. Its bits, bit four, bit thirteen and bit fourteen, become one. The filter now holds eight ones, and no words at all.
Now a question. Is fox in the set? Hash it the same way. bit three, bit five and bit six are all one, so the answer is maybe. And it's right: fox was added.
Is elk in the set? bit zero is zero. If elk had been added, that bit would be one. So the answer is definitely not. As long as no bit is ever cleared, that answer is always right.

Jay was never added. But its bits, bit four, bit six and bit fifteen, were all set by other words. So the filter says maybe. That's a false positive: the one kind of mistake a Bloom filter makes. The more bits are set, the more often it happens.
There's no delete in a Bloom filter. Suppose we try anyway, and clear cat's bits back to zero. But bit six belonged to fox as well.

Now ask for fox again. bit six is zero, so the filter says definitely not, and that's wrong. A Bloom filter must never say no to something it holds. That's why it has no delete. A counting Bloom filter keeps a small counter instead of each bit, so deleting takes away only its own share, as long as you only delete what you really added.
